 ATP Finals Carlos Alcaraz beats Daniil Medvedev in ATP Finals tennis group stage – as it happened
 For the second match in a row Carlos Alcaraz handed out a hiding, Daniil Medvedev going the same way as Francis Tiafoe to all but secure his passage into the last four
  Updated  17m ago Daniel Harris Wed 18 Nov 2026 09.52 EST First published on Wed 18 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Share Key events 18m ago Alcaraz supreme again in hammering Medvedev 
 42m ago Carlos Alcaraz beats Danill Medvedev 6-2 6-4 
 1h ago Alcaraz takes the first set 6-2 against Medvedev 
 3h ago Preamble 
 Carlos Alcaraz celebrates after winning his group stage match against Daniil Medvedev. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters View image in fullscreen Carlos Alcaraz celebrates after winning his group stage match against Daniil Medvedev. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Daniel Harris Wed 18 Nov 2026 09.52 EST First published on Wed 18 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Share From 18m ago 09.50 EST Alcaraz supreme again in hammering Medvedev
 Carlos Alcaraz put on a terrific show in easing past Francis Tiafoe on Monday, but he was facing a man making his debut in this competition. Daniil Medvedev , on the other hand, is a former winner – for all the good it did him, a second opponent wiped off the court in short order 6-2 6-4.
 Though, unlike Tiafoe, broken twice at the outset, Medvedev earned himself a foothold in the match, at 2-2 in the first set Alcaraz took over, taking his opponent’s serve twice in succession while holding twice himself to close out a 6-2 first set.
 For the second match in a row Alcaraz looked impregnable, his return and forehand especially dominant. He broke again at the start of the second set, the match effectively over at that point, and though at 6-2 2-1 he took a medical timeout to have his left thigh heavily bandaged, there was no sense of a problem in how he played or moved, securing the four holds he needed to near enough secure his passage into the last four.
 Well though Alexander Zverev is playing – and it seems inconceivable those won’t be the two finalists – if Alcaraz is fit enough to maintain his current level, he is close to unbeatable.

 1h ago Alcaraz takes the first set 6-2 against Medvedev 
 3h ago Preamble 
 16m ago 09.52 EST Righto, that’s it from us – join us again tomorrow for more. Peace out.
 Share 18m ago 09.50 EST Alcaraz supreme again in hammering Medvedev
 Carlos Alcaraz put on a terrific show in easing past Francis Tiafoe on Monday, but he was facing a man making his debut in this competition. Daniil Medvedev , on the other hand, is a former winner – for all the good it did him, a second opponent wiped off the court in short order 6-2 6-4.
 Though, unlike Tiafoe, broken twice at the outset, Medvedev earned himself a foothold in the match, at 2-2 in the first set Alcaraz took over, taking his opponent’s serve twice in succession while holding twice himself to close out a 6-2 first set.
 For the second match in a row Alcaraz looked impregnable, his return and forehand especially dominant. He broke again at the start of the second set, the match effectively over at that point, and though at 6-2 2-1 he took a medical timeout to have his left thigh heavily bandaged, there was no sense of a problem in how he played or moved, securing the four holds he needed to near enough secure his passage into the last four.
 Well though Alexander Zverev is playing – and it seems inconceivable those won’t be the two finalists – if Alcaraz is fit enough to maintain his current level, he is close to unbeatable.
 Share 25m ago 09.42 EST Asked what he did well, Alcaraz says “everything”. He saw Medvedev serve well in his first match, earning a lot of free points, but he returned really aggressively, hitting deep, and he hit the ball in the sweet spot almost every time. Against Medvedev, you have to be chill because balls keep coming back, but he thinks he was smooth and thought clearly in tough moments.
 Share 32m ago 09.35 EST “It’s like what do you do?” Jamie says of trying to beat Alcaraz. ”I’m perplexed.” Tim agrees, describing him as “faultless”, and he’s operated at a level this week no one, not even Sinner, can match.
 Share 34m ago 09.33 EST Still no word from Alcaraz – for some reason, we’ve not been allowed to enjoy the post-match on-court stuff this week. But apparently he’s imminent.
 Share 37m ago 09.31 EST And who can stop him? Of this field, only Zverev serving like God, and even then.
 Share 37m ago 09.30 EST Alcaraz isn’t quite through to the semis – he’sdhave to lose 1 and 1 to Cobolli, with Medvedev thrashing Tiafoe, to miss out. I daresay he’ll be OK.
 Share 41m ago 09.27 EST I guess we’ll soon find out how his thigh’s doing; every other bit of him seems tip-top.
 Share 42m ago 09.26 EST Carlos Alcaraz beats Danill Medvedev 6-2 6-4
 *Alcaraz 6-2 6-4 Medvedev Alcaraz opens the angle for a run-around forehand down the line … but misses. No matter: another, top-spun cross, makes 15-all, then a wrongfooter opens bare space for the putaway; is his forehand the best shot in the game? I think it might have to be, much as I love Amanda Anisimova’s backhand. Medvedev then goes long on his own forehand, offering two match points, and just as I’m about to type Alcaraz only needs one, he shanks a ball wide to end a rally he was dominating. For all the difference it makes, a big serve forcing the long return and, quite simply we are privileged to be living in Alcaraz’s time. He’s everything a tenniser should be, an aesthetic joy and intellectual inspiration.
 View image in fullscreen Carlos Alcaraz prepares to fire off a forehand during his straight sets victory over Daniil Medvedev. Photograph: Valerio Pennicino/Getty Images Share Updated at  09.29 EST 47m ago 09.20 EST Alcaraz 6-2 5-4 Medvedev* An ace down the middle makes 30-0, but a tremendous return, guided cross, allows a finishing forehand, guided line. An error from Medvedev then donates 30-all, before a return drops fractionally long and a second ace demands Alcaraz serve out the match.
 Share 50m ago 09.18 EST *Alcaraz 6-2 5-3 Medvedev Tim is more worried about Alcaraz’s hammy than Jamie Murray, who’s courtside, saying you don’t strap something heavily if it’s fine and this kind of situation doesn’t improve quickly. Meantime, it’s Medvedev sent lanking to hither and yon as 15-0 becomes 30-0, and ace out wide – the hardest serve to hit from the advantage court – makes 40-15, the Russian unable to assault a tepid second serve in the correct manner, prior to netting a forehand. Alcaraz is a game away.
 Share 55m ago 09.12 EST Alcaraz 6-2 4-3 Medvedev* Medvedev’s second ace of the match makes 30-0, then Alcaraz misses a forehand down the line and a further ace secures the love hold.
 Share 1h ago 09.11 EST *Alcaraz 6-2 4-2 Medvedev Medvedev unloads the suitcase at a serve sent down slowly but way out wide … and misses the baseline. A service winner than makes 30-0, another takes us to 40, and it’s not easy to get running someone not brooking rallies. Medvedev then nets a dropped return, and there’s no sense he can force a way back into this.
 Share 1h ago 09.08 EST Alcaraz 6-2 3-2 Medvedev* At 15-0, Alcaraz opens the court with a violent forehand down the line, only to get lost in the supermarket when attempting to tidy, netting the drop he eventually decides to play. And from there, Medvedev secures a love hold, insecure in the knowledge that the damage is probably done.
 Share 1h ago 09.06 EST *Alcaraz 6-2 3-1 Medvedev Or hope he gets injured! A tactical triumph for Medvedev as Alcaraz takes a medical timeout and the trainer works his left hamstring and thigh, then bandages it up pretty heavily. I guess the aim now will be to keep him moving and, sure enough, Medvedev looks to keep the first rally going … so Alcaraz, in the corner, runs around his backhand to unleash a forehand winner, before taking 30-0 with a drop … and 40 with a volley after Medvedev doesn’t do enough with an attempted pass. Then, at 40-15, he goes long on the backhand and, bandaging aside, there’s no obvious sign of discomfort in the way the Spaniard is moving.
 View image in fullscreen Carlos Alcaraz looks to be in control of the second set too. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Share Updated at  09.15 EST 1h ago 08.59 EST Alcaraz 6-2 2-1 Medvedev* Kevin Pietersen once told me that, when planning how to get out south African batters, they came to Jacques Kallis and all they could come up with was “run out candiate early in his innings”. I’m minded of it because Tim says Medvedev needs to hope Alcaraz gets complacent and loses focus, the desperation similarly fanciful … but a love hold stops the rot of three straight breaks and gets him on the board in set two.
 Share 1h ago 08.56 EST *Alcaraz 6-2 2-0 Medvedev A wrong-footing forehand makes 0-15, then a forehand controlled down the line takes us to 30-all. A big serve is deep in the box, after which Alcaraz tries a drop which clips the top of the net, actually giving Medvedev a chance to run it down. So he does, so he’s passed, then a second serve directed wider than Francis Begbie goes unreturned, and all Medvedev can do is gesticulate in what-can-I-do pose. The answer, I’m afraid, shares the same initials as Super Furry Animals.
 Share 1h ago 08.52 EST Alcaraz 6-2 1-0 Medvedev* The problem opponents have against Alcaraz and Sinner is they deny hope: really, all Medvedev can do is hoe he plays better against an opponent playing worse, because there aren’t really any exploitable flaws, so not much that can be done in a tactical sense. Sure enough, Medvedev comes in to net a volley then, sending down a second serve, hits the middle of the box, so a forehand return arrives at his tootsies before he can adjust. It’s soon 30-all, though, Medvedev leaping backwards to unload an overhead, but another good return, this time of a decent serve provokes the error and raises break point. It’s saved, but on deuce, another aggressive second serve helps not at all, a booming forehand down the line far, far too good, so playing advantage, a decent first serve means a return that sits up. Medvedev, though, can’t put it away and, when both men arrive at the net, the inevitable happens; in a battle of cuteness there’s only one winner, Alcaraz, caressing a forehand winner across the face of the tape. He is so benevolently, wickedly brilliant; it’s a complete outrage, and this match feels 10 to over.
 Share Updated at  08.52 EST 1h ago 08.45 EST Alcaraz takes the first set 6-2 against Medvedev
 *Alcaraz 6-2 Medvedev These last three games encapsulate, in microcosm, the suffocating savagery of Alcaraz. He can play much better than this, but his meh is still so good and his ability to leap on the slightest weakness so resounding that oit demands a level most opponents can’t sustain. He eases to 40-15, then Medvedev goes wide on the backhand, and a set that was close for a bit is emphatic at its end. The runaway train will take some collaring from here.
 View image in fullscreen One down, one to go. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Share Updated at  09.05 EST 1h ago 08.41 EST Alcaraz 5-2 Medvedev* Oh dear: consecutive errors from Medvedev give Alcaraz 0-30, then he ups the pace on a forehand dematerialised cross to the corner; he cleans up easily, then a fine return elicits a netted backhand, and after n engaging start, this set is disappearing quickly.
 Share 1h ago 08.39 EST *Alcaraz 4-2 Medvedev Medvedev blocks balls back them bumrushes the net … which Alcaraz hits via backhand; 0-15. But a poor backhand cedes the advantage, and though Medvedev does well to chase a second serve several miles out of court, it leaves plenty of space for the clean-up winner. However, Alcaraz then nets a forehand. A tremendous rally doth then ensue, Medvedev well in it … until he isn’t, a surprise swiped backhand down the line too good, and it’s beginning to look like one of those matches in which the Spaniard does whatever is asked of him to make sure he wins. A service winner duly seals the consolidation.
 Share 2h ago 08.34 EST Alcaraz 3-2 Medvedev* Medvedev directs a second serve out wide … and Alcaraz times his leap perfectly, hooking a forehand winner cross for 0-15. But though a forehand backed up by a volley makes 15-all, a further error is followed by a double, Medvedev going bigger on second delivery perhaps because of what happened last time, and after a promising start, he’s now down two break points. Of which Alcaraz needs only one, another fine return inciting the error, and we might just be watching the cuddliest, most personable assassin the world has ever seen.
 Share 2h ago 08.30 EST *Alcaraz 2-2 Medvedev Both men are operating at a good level, but after making 15-0 with a swing-volley, Alcaraz sends down a double. Medvedev is hitting well from the back, denying width and air, then he sees the opportunity to attack … but gives it too much. Still, to win this, he’s got to leap on opportunities, and a further baseline rally ends when Alcaraz overhits a backhand; 30-all. He does, though, make 40-30 and Medvedev doesn’t do enough when offered a hittable serve, forcing the issue a couple of shots later to send a forehand long.
 Share 2h ago 08.24 EST Alcaraz 1-2 Medvedev* I mentioned Alcaraz’s wig; Medvedev, meanwhile, has come as the Estonian flag. Back with the match, Medvedev makes 30-§15 with an excellent serve but at 40-30, Alcaraz nails a backhand return for deuce. No matter: a pair of decent first serves secure the hold.
 View image in fullscreen Photograph: Daniel Kopatsch/Getty Images Share 2h ago 08.19 EST *Alcaraz 1-1 Medvedev A high-kicking serve out wide, an ace, is followed by a service winner down the middle; decent work. At 40-0, though, Medvedev reads a second serve, ushering a flat backhand winner down the line, only to then overhit a forehand. Still, he’s playing nicely, looking to take it to Alcaraz, and this could be a really fun tussle.
 Share 2h ago 08.16 EST Alcaraz 0-1 Medvedev* (*denotes server) Alcaraz broke Tiafoe immediately, then again, but I can’t see Medvedev allowing that, and he quickly makes 30-0, then plays a really good point for 40-0, sending his man nashing futilely from corner to corner then, almost from around his arse, he takes a forehand just off the ground to flip a inside-out winner. Excellent start and already, this is more of a contest than Alcaraz’s last match.
 View image in fullscreen Daniil Medvedev has started well. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Share Updated at  09.07 EST 2h ago 08.13 EST Ready … play. 
 Share 2h ago 08.13 EST I call this Vimto sunshine. 
 View image in fullscreen Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP Share 2h ago 08.08 EST Alcaraz wins the toss and, as is the current vogue, seeks to put pressure on his opponent by electing to receive.
 Share 2h ago 08.05 EST Here they come. The crowd are up for this one.
 Share 2h ago 08.03 EST Our players are tunnelling; I enjoy Alcaraz’s colour combination, photo to follow.
 Share 2h ago 08.00 EST It may well be chance, but it’s also the height of Medvedev, a born contrarian. I don’t think he’ll mooch about and wait to lose like Tiafoe did – he’ll try things and, by hitting flat, might deny Alcaraz the leverage he needs to hit with heavy spin.
 Share 2h ago 07.58 EST Who wants a banging stat? Don’t all rush at once. Anyway, here goes: Daniil Medvedev is 0-19 against Djokovic, Sinner, Alcaraz when they’re ranked in the top 10 but not No 1 …but when they are No 1, he’s 8-8.
 Share 2h ago 07.45 EST I’ve just seen Henman’s post-Tiafoe interview with Alcaraz; “I felt fantastic out there,” he said. Oof madone, what it must be like to experience that, and to feel comfortable saying it because it’s self-evidently true.
 I’m going to start conceiving of liveblogging in that way; “Thanks Tim, I’m feeling really mediocre in here.”
 Share 2h ago 07.39 EST In the men’s doubles, Skupski/Harrison, who lost their first match to Putz/Krawietz, have beaten Vavassori/Bolleli so are still in the competition. They’ll probably need a win of Zeballos/Granollers to progress.
 Share 3h ago 07.35 EST On Sky, Tim Henman is kind of saying had Ben Shelton managed to eke out the second-set tiebreak against Zverev, he might’ve made a match of it, but at the same time, he knows that’s the point: everyone knew he was never going to, and in the event, he didn’t get close to doing so.
 Share 3h ago 07.34 EST The problem we have, I think, is that Sinner and Alcaraz are still young, with plenty of scope to improve, while there’s little sense those below Zverev can get better enough to be close. I hope Joao Fonseca can get there, but otherwise it feels like we’re hoping rather than expecting the likes of Rafael Jodar, Moise Kouame and Jakub Mensik to close the gap.
 Share 3h ago 07.00 EST Preamble
 One of the principal reasons we watch sport is because, unlike real life, we don’t know, with crushing and tedious inevitability, what’s going to happen. However that doesn’t feel like the case in men’s tennis at the moment: roughly, if Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz are healthy, one of them wins, but if they aren’t and it’s a tournament that really matters, Alexander Zverev wins.
 And, if this week has shown us anything, it’s that this is even more the case now tan before. Zverev is 2-0 but more telling than that is the the manner of of his wins, neither Arthur Fils nor Ben Shelton able to so much as threaten him – and he has levels in reserve he’s not had to bother seeking.
 Similarly, Carlos Alcaraz devastated Francis Tiafoe in his first match, the gulf in class and intensity chasmic. Tiafoe couldn’t even rustle up the aggression to get down on himself because he knew he was helpless.
 On the face of things, our match this afternoon feels like more of the same. Except Daniil Medvedev is the maverick’s maverick, capable of the best and worst, in play and attitude – sometimes during the same rally. In typical style, he’s been brutal in explaining how little he wants to be playing this tournament and yet, now that he is, he can’t be discounted. He’s already beaten Alcaraz on hards this season – albeit outdoors – and presents a unique challenge, able to stand way out of court because of how unusually his movement belies his height. If he’s at it, he’ll make this interesting and fun; if he isn’t, it’ll be over quicksmart – yet still fun, because Alcaraz can do no other, one aspect of overwhelming predictability we can all embrace.
 Play: 2pm local, 1pm GMT
